I'm Yash, and last year I gave Aadhya a 2 out of 5 in our final-year project peer rating. I still think about it.
We were a team of four building a water-quality sensor for the college lake. From August to February, Aadhya did most of the real work. She wrote the code, fixed the sensor when it fried, and stayed late when the rest of us went home.
Then in March her grandmother fell ill and she went home to Nagpur for the last two weeks. The rest of us rushed the report and the demo. When the rating form came, all I could see was those two weeks: her empty chair, the late nights we did without her.
Two, I typed. Missed the final phase.
In May I scrolled back through our group chat to find a file, and it was all her messages. Month after month.

qa.q: What score did Yash give Aadhya in the peer rating?
qa.a: Yash gave Aadhya a 2 out of 5.

qa.q: Why did a 2 feel fair to Yash when filling in the form?
qa.a: The last two weeks without Aadhya were the freshest and most stressful memory, so her empty chair crowded out the six months when she did most of the real work.

qa.q: What could Yash do before rating a teammate next time?
qa.a: Yash could look back over the whole project, for example by scrolling the group chat or listing each month, before letting the final weeks decide the score.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when she sees a 2 after carrying the project for months?
qa.a: Aadhya would likely feel hurt and unfairly judged, especially since she was away for a family reason and had done most of the work before that.

grounding: It shows a student rating a team member mostly on the last few weeks, so recent absence dominates the overall impression.

Course coordinator's note, end-of-semester feedback (Kishore)
Ujjwal, 20, gave our twelve-week pottery workshop 1 out of 5, with the comment: "Badly run, rushed, room was unbearable."
The last two weeks were hard. The fan in the studio broke, and we squeezed two sessions into one to finish before exams. His complaint about those weeks is fair.
But in his mid-semester form, Ujjwal wrote: "Best class I've taken. I look forward to it every week." He made eleven pieces, more than anyone, and brought his cousin to the open studio in week 6.
I met him and showed him both forms side by side. He read them, laughed a little, and said, "Honestly I only remembered the heat."
Next: we'll collect short feedback every three weeks, so the final form isn't just the last fortnight, and the fan is being repaired.

qa.q: What score did Ujjwal give the pottery workshop?
qa.a: He gave it 1 out of 5.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's comment "I only remembered the heat" suggest about how he judged the course?
qa.a: It suggests the uncomfortable last two weeks felt like the whole course to him, pushing aside the weeks he enjoyed and the eleven pieces he made.

qa.q: Which step by Kishore helped, and why?
qa.a: Showing Ujjwal both forms side by side, so he could see his own earlier praise and notice how much the last weeks had coloured his rating.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel reading the 1 out of 5?
qa.a: Kishore may feel stung, since he knows how much Ujjwal loved the class for most of the term, while also accepting that the last weeks were genuinely hard.

grounding: It shows a student rating a course almost entirely on the last few weeks, so recent problems dominate the overall impression.

On the third floor of the courier office in Kolkata, Pallavi, twenty-six, had one evening to write six annual reviews. She opened the small green notebook she had kept since January: one line per person, every month.
She started with Uday. Her memory said: December was a mess. He had misrouted forty parcels in the festival rush and snapped at a driver. She could still feel how angry she had been.
The notebook said more. March: "Built the new route sheet, cut delays." May: "Trained two new joiners, patient." August: "Covered night shifts for a week, no complaints." October: "Found the billing error." December: "Misrouted parcels in rush; tired, overworked?"
Pallavi put down her pen. Eleven good months and one hard one.
She wrote the December problem into the review, clearly, with a plan. Then she wrote the rest of the year too.

qa.q: How many parcels had Uday misrouted in December?
qa.a: He had misrouted forty parcels in the festival rush.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling about Uday before she opened the notebook?
qa.a: She still felt angry about December, and her memory was painting his whole year by that one bad month.

qa.q: Which habit made Pallavi's review fair?
qa.a: Keeping one line per person every month, so the review could show Uday's route sheet, training and night shifts alongside the December problem.

qa.q: What would change for Uday if Pallavi had written the review from memory alone?
qa.a: Uday would likely get a poor review based on one festival month, which would feel unfair after eleven months of good work and might make him give up trying.

grounding: It shows a fair manager using notes from the whole year so a review reflects all months, not only the latest memory.

Joseph, you think the Class 10 list is hard? Come, let your Anjali aunty tell you about your father at fifteen.
Babu had to learn the twenty-two fundamental duties for his civics exam. Every night he started at number one, and every night he fell asleep somewhere around eight. In the exam he wrote the first six perfectly, word for word, and then made up the rest. The teacher wrote "a strong start" in red.

Mock interview volunteer's note, Friday (Naveen, final year)
I sat on the panel for Farhan's mock interview for the bank internship. He walked in, bumped the chair, dropped his file, and his first words were, "Sorry, sorry, I'm so bad at this."
I watched the two faculty members on the panel. One stopped taking notes after that line. For the next ten minutes Farhan actually gave good answers, a clear one about budgeting for his college fest, but the panel kept asking him, "Are you sure?"

Weird evening at the café. Urmila's family had set up a first meeting with a guy called Rohan, and she asked me to sit two tables away "just in case".
He was twenty minutes late. He came in sweating, phone in hand, and the first thing he said was about the traffic being "absolutely useless". I saw Urmila's face close like a shutter.

They do. But I think both of them lost the evening in the first minute. Rohan could have walked in calmer. Urmila could have let the next forty minutes count.
— Sumit

passage:
I'm Jatin, and I worked under Ramesh on the hospital billing software project for six hard months. Late nights, one angry client, two people quitting.
On the last day, I expected a quick email saying "Project closed." Instead Ramesh booked the terrace for the final half hour and brought samosas.
He didn't make a speech about the problems. He went round the circle and said one specific thing to each person. To me: "You stayed until two a.m. the night the server crashed, and you never once complained." To Farida: "Your test checklist is now the company standard." Then he said clearly what would happen next: who would support the client, who was moving to the new team.
People went down the stairs smiling. Two weeks later, when someone asked me how the project was, I said, "Tough, but good." I think the terrace is why.

qa.q: What did Ramesh bring to the terrace?
qa.a: He brought samosas.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's choice of a terrace meeting suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests he knew people would remember the end most, and wanted a tough project to finish on a warm, clear note instead of a cold email.

qa.q: Which parts of Ramesh's ending worked, and why?
qa.a: Thanking each person for something specific and then stating clearly who would do what next, so people left feeling valued and not confused about the future.

qa.q: How does the ending change the way Jatin remembers the project?
qa.a: Jatin now sums it up as "Tough, but good", because the warm final half hour stays with Jatin more than the late nights.

grounding: It shows a caring leader ending a hard project on a warm, clear note, knowing people will remember the high point and the finish.

passage:
Week 1, Sunday: Avni, twenty-five, ran her first free art class for colony children in the community hall. It went well until the last ten minutes: paint water spilled, parents arrived early, and everyone left in a rush. Kashish, her helper, heard one boy tell his mother, "It was messy."
Week 2, Sunday: Avni kept the same painting, but at ten to five she rang a small bell. The children put down brushes, sat in a circle, and each held up one thing they were proud of. They sang a short goodbye song. Avni said clearly, "Next week, we paint the sky." Clean-up happened with music.
Week 3, Sunday: Kashish counted twenty-two children, eight more than the first week. A mother told Avni, "She talked about the circle all week." Avni smiled and moved the bell to the front table, where she wouldn't forget it.

qa.q: How many children came in Week 3?
qa.a: Twenty-two children, eight more than the first week.

qa.q: What did Avni want when she added the bell and the circle?
qa.a: She wanted the class to finish on a warm, clear note, so the children would remember feeling proud rather than the rush and the spills.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Ringing the bell for a proud-moment circle, a goodbye song and a clear "Next week, we paint the sky" gave the class a good ending and a reason to come back.

qa.q: How might the boy who said "It was messy" remember the class if he came back in Week 2?
qa.a: He would likely remember showing his painting in the circle and singing, so the class would feel fun and calm instead of messy.

grounding: It shows a caring leader ending a class on a warm, clear note, knowing people will remember the high point and the finish.
